To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a) a model based on biased competition mechanisms and a multiplicative gain-control is able to reproduce the main psychophysical results about selective visual attention, b) the neurodynamics of spatial and object attention is achieved by a multiplicative interaction between the modules of the dorsal and the ventral path of visual processing and c) the neurodynamical control of spatial resolution is implemented by the latency difference between neurons of V1 that are sensitive to different spatial frequencies.

the neurodynamics of the proposed multimodular system can explain: (1) the emergence of a multiplicative gain modulation in a system of mutually biased coupled modules; (2) the emergence of spatial and object selective visual attention; (3) the emergence of the resolution hypothesis; and (4) the emergence of different latencies in V1 depending on the spatial resolution of the visual scene.

the biased competition mechanism can be modelled by a dynamical system of neural modules which are related to the different areas of dorsal and ventral stream of the visual cortex and that this model can explain the resolution hypothesis.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a computational model of visual selective attention that includes the main experimental evidence of the biased competition theory, the resolution hypothesis and a neurodynamically plausible implementation of the model.
the development of a computational model for visual attention that is able to explain several psychophysical and neurophysiological results.

the development of a computational model for the neurodynamics of visual attention in which spatial and object attention emerge dynamically from a multiplicative coupling between different cortical modules.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our model is able to account for the most important experimental results related with the biased competition hypothesis and the resolution hypothesis.
the proposed model is able to reproduce the main psychophysical findings related with the biased competition hypothesis and the resolution hypothesis.

the model presented here can be considered as a first step towards a computational model of selective visual processing in natural scenes which can be related to the neuroanatomy of the visual cortex and to its psychophysiological properties.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed a computational model of selective visual spatial and object attention based on the biased competition hypothesis and we have incorporated the resolution hypothesis in order to explain how spatial and object attention are related with the neurodynamics of spatial resolution in visual scenes.
the model proposed here provides a neurodynamically plausible explanation for the biased competition hypothesis, and also, for a mechanism that can account for the resolution hypothesis.

a multimodular neurodynamical system can account for the biased competition hypothesis and the resolution hypothesis in a unified framework for the explanation of the neurodynamical mechanisms for selective visual attention.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the neurodynamical mechanisms for the selection of relevant information from natural visual scenes can be formulated in a multimodular system where the different modules interact through mutual biased coupling.
the neurodynamics of a multimodular neural system is a suitable framework for the implementation of a computational model of visual attention based on biased competition mechanisms.
the neurodynamical system is capable of explaining a wide range of psychophysical phenomena in the visual attention domain.
